title: Questioning Coaching 2026
author: Adam Boxer
summary: Adam Boxer, science teacher and co-owner of Carousel, examines instructional coaching — 'the current Big Thing in teacher development' — and argues that while its evidence base is genuinely strong, translating that evidence into real school practice runs into eight substantial barriers. He walks through psychological problems (coaching creates an implicit two- or three-tier hierarchy of coaches, coachees, and everyone else, which breeds resentment even when leaders insist it implies nothing about competence), definitional confusion (multiple training providers use the term 'instructional coaching' for contradictory practices), and the high financial cost of releasing staff to observe and be observed. He also raises less obvious barriers: coaching depends on coaches being expert 'radiologists' of classroom practice, schools rarely have a shared definition of what good teaching looks like, the 'best' teachers pulled into coaching roles aren't necessarily the best coaches, coaching models poorly serve highly expert teachers who need a different kind of feedback, and schools tend to measure whether coaching is happening rather than whether teaching is actually improving. Boxer discloses that he co-owns a CPD platform that is a direct alternative to instructional coaching, but insists he has tried to evaluate coaching on its merits. His conclusion is not that instructional coaching should be abandoned, but that leaders adopting it wholesale should treat these eight challenges as a serious implementation checklist rather than an afterthought.
points: Boxer's core claim: instructional coaching is well-evidenced as a form of teacher CPD, but implementation in 'the messy reality of schools' faces at least eight distinct psychological, definitional, financial, and practical barriers.

Formalising coaching relationships creates an unavoidable two- or three-tier status hierarchy among staff, and leaders are consistently surprised when well-motivated colleagues respond badly to being designated coachees.
Different training providers claim the same term 'instructional coaching' for opposite practices, which Boxer says renders the term almost completely meaningless and invites lethal mutation at scale.

A back-of-envelope cost model — 20 coaches at an hour a week plus 40 coachees at half an hour each — works out to roughly 1.7 extra teacher salaries (~£86,700/year) for a typical 60-teacher secondary school.

Coaching often substitutes a measurable proxy (is coaching happening) for the actual goal (is teaching improving), and Boxer notes he has personally never once received feedback on the pedagogical quality of his own coaching advice.
quotes: By instituting Instructional coaching, you create a two-tier system, and should not be surprised that people placed on the second tier do not respond well.

Leaders stand up in the hall and say things like 'everyone is going to be coached, and it's about everyone improving regardless of their starting points,' and are subsequently surprised to learn that what colleagues hear is 'you are not good at teaching, and need coaching.'

The term 'instructional coaching' struggles with a lack of a clear definition. Evidence Based Education's Professor Rob Coe notes a number of conflicting definitions of the term, and even where some definitions are similar, the emphasis is often on different aspects and processes.

That's a total of 40 teaching hours a week that will need to get made up somehow, and with typical teachers teaching for 24 hours a week, we end up with an average secondary needing to employ 1.7 new teachers.

Instructional Coaching simply cannot work if the coach is not a highly skilled observer of teaching. I've previously referred to such a person as a 'radiologist', someone who can perceive details and elements that would pass completely unseen by a more casual observer.

The thing we are interested in isn't 'is Instructional Coaching happening?' That's just a proxy. The thing we are really interested in is 'is teaching improving?' Often though, the proxy becomes the measure.
